PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 51 — Lesson 75: Behavioral Health Assessment

FNP-level goal: Assess depression, anxiety, mania/hypomania, psychosis, substance-related symptoms, trauma-related concerns, cognitive change, and suicide risk with a nonjudgmental, trauma-informed, medically aware approach. Build a differential that includes medical and medication causes, determine immediate safety and disposition, and establish a closed-loop outpatient plan when outpatient care is appropriate.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate screening from diagnostic assessment and use validated tools as conversation starters rather than stand-alone diagnoses.
  • Perform a focused mental-status examination and recognize changes requiring urgent medical or psychiatric evaluation.
  • Assess suicide risk directly, respectfully, and systematically while considering thoughts, intent, plan, behavior, access to lethal means, protective factors, and current context.
  • Identify red flags for mania, psychosis, delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, violence risk, and inability to care for basic needs.
  • Connect behavioral symptoms to medical illness, medication effects, trauma, sleep, substance use, social stress, and access barriers.
  • Create a safe disposition and follow-up plan that includes documentation, crisis resources, safety planning when appropriate, and result/referral ownership.

Part 1 — Safety and Medical Stability Come First

Behavioral symptoms can be the first sign of a psychiatric condition, a medical emergency, medication toxicity, intoxication/withdrawal, delirium, trauma, infection, endocrine disease, neurologic disease, hypoxia, or metabolic disturbance. Begin with vital signs, appearance, airway/breathing/circulation concerns, glucose when clinically indicated, level of consciousness, orientation, hydration, pain, recent injury, medication/substance exposure, and acute medical symptoms.

Emergency evaluation is needed for imminent risk of self-harm or harm to others, a recent serious attempt, severe intoxication/withdrawal, delirium or fluctuating consciousness, severe agitation with inability to maintain safety, command hallucinations with unsafe behavior, grave disability/inability to meet basic needs, or concerning medical instability. Do not frame an unstable patient as “only anxious” or delay medical assessment because they have a psychiatric history.

Part 2 — Create a Respectful Space for Disclosure

Use calm, direct, non-stigmatizing language. Explain confidentiality and its limits before a sensitive assessment, including the circumstances in which immediate safety requires action. Ask what matters to the patient, what has changed, what they hope will improve, and whether there are cultural, language, disability, financial, transportation, caregiving, housing, immigration, or privacy barriers affecting care. Use a qualified interpreter when needed; do not rely on family members for sensitive interpretation.

A patient may present with headache, insomnia, GI symptoms, pain, fatigue, poor concentration, palpitations, medication refill requests, or repeated urgent visits rather than the words “depression” or “anxiety.” The FNP’s task is to recognize the pattern without reducing the patient to a diagnosis or overlooking an organic cause.

Part 3 — The Core Behavioral-Health History

Clarify onset, duration, progression, episodic versus persistent course, functional impairment, sleep, energy, concentration, appetite/weight, psychomotor change, mood, anhedonia, irritability, anxiety/panic, trauma symptoms, compulsions, hallucinations, delusions, suspiciousness, dissociation, and cognitive symptoms. Ask about prior diagnoses, therapy, hospitalizations, medications and adherence, prior adverse reactions, family history, pregnancy/postpartum state when relevant, medical illness, and legal/occupational stressors.

Substance history must include alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, sedatives, opioids, nicotine, prescribed medications, nonprescribed substances, supplements, amount/frequency, last use, withdrawal history, overdose history, and readiness for help. A substance history is a routine part of medical safety, not a test of character. Symptoms that occur only during intoxication/withdrawal or after a medication change may have a different pathway than a primary mood or psychotic disorder.

Part 4 — Mental-Status Examination: Observe and Describe

The mental-status examination is a structured description of the patient’s current functioning. Document appearance/behavior, cooperation, level of consciousness, speech, mood, affect, thought process, thought content, perception, cognition/attention/orientation, insight, judgment, and reliability. Describe observable findings before interpreting them: for example, “speech was pressured and difficult to interrupt” is stronger documentation than “patient was manic” before a complete assessment.

Disorganized thought, hallucinations, fixed delusional content, grossly impaired judgment, fluctuating attention, new cognitive change, or markedly altered behavior should expand the differential. A normal brief conversation does not exclude risk; privacy, collateral information where permitted, timeline, and functional decline may reveal what a short examination misses.

Part 5 — Depression: Assess Symptoms, Function, and Danger

Depression may include persistent low mood or loss of interest, sleep/appetite change, fatigue, impaired concentration, guilt/worthlessness, psychomotor change, and thoughts of death or suicide. Symptoms can co-occur with chronic pain, diabetes, heart disease, cancer, neurologic disease, pregnancy/postpartum changes, trauma, and medication effects. Determine duration, severity, impairment, psychotic symptoms, past mania/hypomania, substance use, and safety rather than equating a positive symptom screen with a final diagnosis.

Ask directly about suicide. Direct questioning does not create suicidal thoughts; it opens a safety-relevant conversation. A patient with depression who has psychosis, inability to eat/drink, severe functional decline, current suicidal thoughts, recent attempt, escalating substance use, or unreliable support needs a higher-acuity assessment. The FNP must also assess whether medical causes such as anemia, thyroid disease, sleep disorders, medication effects, or delirium are contributing.

Part 6 — Anxiety and Panic: Exclude the Dangerous Mimics

Anxiety can involve excessive worry, restlessness, tension, irritability, sleep difficulty, poor concentration, panic symptoms, avoidance, and somatic complaints. Panic symptoms may include palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort, dizziness, trembling, nausea, or fear of losing control. These symptoms overlap with acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, asthma, hypoglycemia, thyroid disease, medication/substance effects, withdrawal, and other illnesses.

Do not diagnose panic disorder before assessing the presenting physiology and red flags. New chest pain, syncope, severe dyspnea, focal neurologic symptoms, abnormal vital signs, new-onset symptoms in a high-risk patient, or a concerning medication/substance history requires a medical diagnostic pathway. When anxiety is the working diagnosis, assess triggers, avoidance, impairment, safety, comorbid depression/substance use, and evidence-based therapy/referral access.

Part 7 — Screen for Bipolar Spectrum Before Treating Depression

Depressive episodes may occur in bipolar disorder. Ask about past periods of elevated or unusually irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased energy/activity, rapid or pressured speech, racing thoughts, impulsive/risky behavior, grandiosity, hospitalization, psychosis, and family history. Determine whether symptoms represented a clear change from baseline and caused impairment, not simply a productive or happy period.

Acute mania or psychosis can impair judgment and safety. Severe agitation, inability to sleep for days, escalating risky behavior, psychosis, suicidal or violent intent, or inability to care for self requires urgent psychiatric/emergency assessment. Avoid making a medication change based solely on a depression score if the history suggests bipolar-spectrum illness; treatment planning should follow current guidance and consultation pathways.

Part 8 — Psychosis, Delirium, and Cognitive Change

Psychosis can include hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought/behavior, or marked loss of reality testing. It can occur with primary psychiatric illness, severe mood disorders, substances, medications, neurologic disease, autoimmune/infectious disease, metabolic/endocrine disorders, or delirium. New-onset psychosis, late-life onset, acute onset, fluctuating attention, fever, focal neurologic findings, trauma, or abnormal vital signs should prompt strong consideration of medical causes.

Delirium is an acute disturbance in attention and awareness that often fluctuates. It is a medical emergency until evaluated. Distinguish it from chronic dementia, depression, or a stable psychiatric disorder by asking about baseline cognition, time course, acute illness, medication changes, infection, hypoxia, urinary retention/constipation, pain, and substance exposure. Never dismiss fluctuating confusion as “behavioral.”

Part 9 — Suicide-Risk Assessment: Direct, Structured, and Human

When indicated by screening, symptoms, history, or clinical concern, ask directly about thoughts of death or suicide; timing, frequency, intensity, and duration; intent; any plan; preparatory behavior; previous attempts; self-injury; current stressors; intoxication; access to lethal means; and reasons for living/protective supports. Assess whether the patient can collaborate with a safety plan and whether their environment is safe. Protective factors matter but do not erase acute risk.

Risk assessment is not a checklist that generates an automatic disposition. It requires clinical judgment, current presentation, collateral information when appropriate and permitted, local policy, and access to timely services. A patient with current suicidal thoughts and imminent intent, a recent serious attempt, inability to maintain safety, or severe intoxication/psychosis should not be left alone to arrange routine outpatient follow-up. In the United States, 988 offers 24/7 crisis support by call, text, or chat; call 911 or go to an emergency department for immediate danger or medical emergency.

Part 10 — Safety Planning and Follow-Up Are Clinical Interventions

When outpatient management is clinically appropriate, develop a collaborative, individualized safety plan according to local policy and clinician competence. It may identify warning signs, internal coping strategies, supportive people/settings, professional/community crisis contacts, and steps to reduce access to lethal means. A “no-suicide contract” is not a substitute for a comprehensive assessment, a practical safety plan, appropriate disposition, or follow-up.

Confirm the patient has the crisis/contact information, transportation/telehealth access, a reachable follow-up plan, medication safety instructions, and consent-based support involvement when appropriate. Document risk/protective factors, questions asked, clinical rationale, safety-plan elements, consultation, disposition, and the plan for follow-up contact. A referral without confirmation of access is not a completed plan.

Part 11 — Substance Use and Co-Occurring Conditions

Assess substance use as a possible cause, consequence, or co-occurring condition. Withdrawal from alcohol, sedatives, or other substances can be medically dangerous; stimulant intoxication can contribute to agitation, chest symptoms, psychosis, or hyperthermia; opioid use increases overdose risk; and alcohol/cannabis can worsen sleep, mood, anxiety, cognition, and medication interactions. Ask about overdose prevention, prescription monitoring according to policy, medication combinations, and readiness for treatment.

Do not require sobriety before listening to a patient’s psychiatric symptoms, and do not assume all symptoms are substance-induced. Coordinate urgent medical, addiction, psychiatric, and social-service pathways according to severity. Address harm reduction, overdose safety, and follow-up with current local and national guidance rather than relying on this educational lesson as a treatment protocol.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Depression With Current Suicide Risk

A 31-year-old presents with worsening depression, insomnia, escalating alcohol use, and current thoughts of suicide. They report feeling unable to stay safe if they go home.

FNP reasoning: conduct an immediate direct risk assessment, do not leave the patient alone, activate the clinic’s emergency/crisis protocol, and arrange emergency psychiatric evaluation. A routine referral or a promise to call later is not an adequate response to inability to maintain safety.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: “Panic” With Medical Red Flags

A 58-year-old with diabetes develops sudden chest pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis, and severe anxiety. They have no prior panic diagnosis.

FNP reasoning: anxiety does not exclude acute coronary syndrome or another medical emergency. Assess vital signs and use the appropriate emergency cardiac pathway rather than diagnosing panic from the emotional presentation.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: New Confusion and Hallucinations

An 80-year-old with no prior psychotic disorder develops abrupt visual hallucinations, inattention, and fluctuating confusion after a new medication and urinary symptoms.

FNP reasoning: this is delirium until evaluated, with infection, medication effect, urinary retention, metabolic disturbance, and other medical causes in the differential. Arrange urgent medical assessment rather than treating it as new primary psychosis.

FNP Behavioral-Health Assessment Framework

  1. Stabilize first: evaluate medical danger, intoxication/withdrawal, delirium, agitation, and immediate self/other-harm risk.
  2. Create safety for disclosure: explain confidentiality limits, use respectful language, protect privacy, and address access barriers.
  3. Build the timeline: onset, course, function, sleep, mood, anxiety, psychosis, trauma, substances, medications, and medical illness.
  4. Perform a mental-status examination: describe behavior, speech, affect, thought, perception, cognition, insight, and judgment.
  5. Assess suicide risk directly: ideation, intent, plan, behavior, means access, acute stressors, supports, ability to maintain safety, and clinical context.
  6. Exclude dangerous mimics: ACS, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, thyroid/endocrine disease, medication toxicity, infection, neurologic disease, and delirium.
  7. Close the loop: crisis plan, emergency precautions, safety-plan elements when appropriate, referrals actually accessible to the patient, follow-up contact, and careful documentation.

High-Yield Summary

Behavioral symptoms: may be psychiatric, medical, substance-related, medication-related, or all of these at once.
Depression: assess function, psychosis, past mania/hypomania, medical causes, substances, and suicide risk—not only a screening score.
Anxiety/panic: do not miss cardiopulmonary, endocrine, neurologic, metabolic, medication, or substance causes.
Mania/psychosis: impaired judgment, severe agitation, unsafe behavior, inability to care for self, or new/late-life onset may need urgent assessment.
Delirium: acute fluctuating attention/awareness is a medical emergency until evaluated.
Suicide risk: ask directly and use clinical judgment; acute risk requires immediate action, not a routine referral.
FNP standard: combine compassion, diagnostic humility, medical assessment, direct safety inquiry, clear disposition, and closed-loop continuity.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Behavioral-health assessment, suicide-risk management, crisis response, medication decisions, involuntary-treatment processes, consultation, and emergency disposition must follow current evidence, local law/policy, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation. If you or someone else is in immediate danger in the United States, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department; for crisis support, call/text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.
